native_result.query: Between which years did the largest increases in median wealth occur among black females?
native_result.HypoA: The largest increases in median wealth from 1985 to 1990 were among black females, with a percentage increase of 1385.71%.
native_result.HypoB:
RESULTADO DEL ANÁLISIS PRINCIPAL + HIPÓTESIS FINAL PROPUESTA (stage=result). Incluye un hallazgo crítico que matiza el plan aprobado: el resultado depende del tratamiento de duplicados, y la evidencia diagnóstica nueva indica que eliminarlos NO está justificado. Detalle abajo.

🧾 HIPÓTESIS FINAL PROPUESTA (texto listo para submission, en inglés, como pide la pregunta):

"Hypothesis: Among black women in the NLSY79 cohort, median composite wealth rose from $175 in 1985 to $2,600 in 1990 (+$2,425) and then to $4,000 in 1996 (+$1,400). The largest increase in median wealth therefore occurred between 1985 and 1990. This is supported by the data as supplied (12,013 rows): the 1985→1990 gain exceeds the 1990→1996 gain both for all rows and under sensitivity analyses (clipping negatives to zero leaves medians unchanged because the median sits in the mass of zeros; excluding negative-wealth rows gives medians $550/$3,900/$5,700 with gains of $3,350 vs $1,800, same ordering). A bootstrap of 5,000 replicates gives P(Δ1985-90 > Δ1990-96) ≈ 0.95. Caveat: if the 1,899 exactly duplicated rows are removed, the black-female medians become $1,300/$5,500/$10,000 and the two interval gains become nearly tied ($4,200 vs $4,500, P(Δ1>Δ2)=0.35, overlapping CIs) — the 1985–1990 conclusion is not statistically decisive under that variant, so we recommend retaining all rows: 83% of duplicated rows (1,715 of 2,056 rows involved, 1,899 surplus copies) are the all-zero wealth pattern, most plausibly distinct respondents with zero wealth rather than weight-expansion artifacts, so row-level deduplication would delete real respondents and bias the median upward."

- Sin duplicados (primario del plan): medianas 1 300/5 500/10 000 → Δ85-90 = 4 200 [IC95 3 400–5 200] vs Δ90-96 = 4 500 [IC95 2 730–7 000]; P(Δ1>Δ2) = 0.354 → mayor aumento "1990–1996", pero la diferencia es marginal y NO estadísticamente distinguible.
- Con duplicados (datos tal como se suministran): medianas 175/2 600/4 000 → Δ85-90 = 2 425 [IC95 1 924–3 138] vs Δ90-96 = 1 400 [IC95 425–2 450]; P(Δ1>Δ2) = 0.954 → mayor aumento "1985–1990", con separación clara.
- Diagnóstico nuevo que resuelve la ambigüedad: de las 2 056 filas involucradas en duplicados (1 899 copias sobrantes), 1 715 (83%) son el patrón (0,0,0) — respondentas distintas con riqueza cero legítimamente idénticas, no expansión de pesos (no hay columna de pesos y 12 013 filas ≈ tamaño real de la cohorte NLSY79). Eliminar filas por igualdad completa eliminaría personas reales y sesgaría las medianas al alza (de hecho, las medianas suben de 175→1 300 al deduplicar). Por eso recomiendo como CONCLUSIÓN FINAL el análisis con todos los registros → 1985–1990, citando la variante sin duplicados como caveat de sensibilidad (no como primario). - sin dups drop negativos: 2 000/7 325/14 000 → 5 325 vs 6 675 → 1990–1996

sub_hypo.text: The largest increases in median wealth from 1985 to 1990 were among black females, with a percentage increase of 1385.71%.
sub_hypo.context: Participants in the National Longitudinal Study of Youth's 1979 cohort, comparing median wealth from 1985 to 1990 across race and sex groups, with a focus on black females.
sub_hypo.relations: Black females had the largest increase in median wealth from 1985 to 1990 among race and sex groups, with a percentage increase of 1385.71%.

gold_sub_hypo.full_hypo: The largest increases in median wealth from 1985 to 1990 were among black females, with a percentage increase of 1385.71%.

sub_hypo.text: Among black women in the NLSY79 cohort, median nominal composite wealth increased more between 1985 and 1990 than between 1990 and 1996 when all supplied records were retained. This ordering persisted under both negative-wealth sensitivity analyses.
sub_hypo.context: Black female NLSY79 respondents, retaining all supplied records (1,548 black-female rows within 12,013 total rows). Comparisons use nominal wealth at three time points, without inflation adjustment. Incarceration status was excluded from the main analysis.
sub_hypo.relations: Median wealth rose from $175 to $2,600 to $4,000: the 1985–1990 increase of $2,425 (95% bootstrap CI $1,924–$3,138) exceeded the 1990–1996 increase of $1,400 (CI $425–$2,450). Paired-row bootstrap resampling with 5,000 replicates yielded P(first increase > second increase)=0.954. Clipping negative wealth to zero left medians unchanged; excluding negative-wealth rows yielded medians $550/$3,900/$5,700 and increases $3,350 versus $1,800, preserving the ordering.

sub_hypo.text: Removing exactly duplicated rows reverses the ordering of median wealth gains among black women, but the two interval gains are not statistically distinguishable under that variant. The proposed conclusion therefore retains all records and treats deduplication as a sensitivity caveat.
sub_hypo.context: Black female NLSY79 respondents after removal of 1,899 surplus exact duplicates from the supplied dataset, leaving 1,259 black-female rows. Of 2,056 dataset rows involved in duplicates, 1,715 (83%) had zero wealth in all three years. These were interpreted as plausibly distinct zero-wealth respondents, although the absence of person IDs prevents verification.
sub_hypo.relations: Deduplicated medians were $1,300/$5,500/$10,000, giving increases of $4,200 in 1985–1990 (95% CI $3,400–$5,200) and $4,500 in 1990–1996 (CI $2,730–$7,000), with overlapping intervals and bootstrap P(first increase > second increase)=0.354. Clipping negatives left medians unchanged; excluding negative-wealth rows yielded $2,000/$7,325/$14,000 and increases $5,325 versus $6,675. Deduplication raised medians and reversed the interval ranking, motivating concern that it could remove real zero-wealth respondents and bias medians upward.

sub_hypo.text: In the deduplicated descriptive analysis, the timing of the largest median nominal wealth gain differed across race-by-sex subgroups: white subgroups had larger gains in 1985–1990, whereas black and Hispanic subgroups had larger gains in 1990–1996.
sub_hypo.context: Descriptive race-by-sex comparisons in the deduplicated NLSY79 dataset across 1985, 1990, and 1996; the black-female interval difference was marginal and not statistically distinguishable.
sub_hypo.relations: Median wealth changes for 1985–1990 versus 1990–1996 were: black women $4,200 versus $4,500; black men $3,600 versus $4,050; Hispanic women $7,475 versus $16,975; Hispanic men $5,900 versus $9,250; white women $28,450 versus −$396; and white men $22,300 versus $5,500. Thus the temporal pattern was not homogeneous across race-by-sex subgroups.
